905.title: Agriculture
905.tag: Agriculture: growing crops and animals are inventory-like costs; cooperatives and patrons have special rules.
905.truth: A farmer's costs build up in crops and herds long before anything is sold, so growing crops and developing animals accumulate cost like inventory, and long-lived orchards and breeding animals are depreciated like equipment. Cooperatives return earnings to member-patrons based on business done, which is why patronage allocations have their own accounting.

analogy.title: The Backyard Apple Tree
analogy.story: The seeds, fertilizer and water you pour into this year's apples are the cost of this year's harvest. The apple tree itself, which will fruit for 20 years, is equipment — its cost is spread over those harvests.

recognition: Capitalize costs of growing crops and developing animals held for sale as inventory; expense costs of normal operations when incurred (905-330).
Permanent land development costs are not depreciated; orchards, vineyards and production animals are capitalized during development and depreciated once productive (905-360).
Cooperatives record patronage refunds to members; patrons recognize allocations when notified (905-325).
Source library holds the Overall subtopic (905-10); the industry subtopics (905-330, 905-360, etc.) are referenced there.

measurement.basis: Lower of cost and net realizable value (inventory); cost less depreciation (productive assets)
measurement.initial: Accumulate direct and indirect production costs.
measurement.subsequent: Harvested crops may be carried at NRV when immediately marketable at quoted prices, per industry practice.

journalEntries.label: Capitalize crop-growing costs
journalEntries.scenario: A grower spends $180,000 on seed, fertilizer and labor for this season's crop.
journalEntries.memo: Relieved to cost of sales when the harvest is sold.

auditTraps.q: Is a vineyard's development cost expensed?
auditTraps.a: No — capitalized during development and depreciated over its productive life once commercially productive.

auditTraps.q: Can harvested commodities be carried above cost?
auditTraps.a: Industry practice permits NRV for harvested crops with immediate marketability at quoted prices and insignificant disposal costs.

auditTraps.q: Are patronage dividends from a coop revenue for the member?
auditTraps.a: They reduce the member's cost of purchases (or are income if related to sales), recognized when allocated.

908.title: Airlines
908.tag: Airlines: industry scope for revenue cycle, flight equipment and maintenance (overview in this source).
908.truth: Airlines sell tickets long before flights, own fleets of mobile equipment and must maintain them under strict schedules. The industry Topic points to how these realities interact with general GAAP: tickets are contract liabilities (air traffic liability) until flown, aircraft are depreciated by component, and maintenance policies must be applied consistently.

analogy.title: The Concert Tour Bus Company
analogy.story: A bus company sells tour seats months ahead, owns buses that are always on the road, and must rebuild engines every few years. It earns the fare when the trip happens, and plans for overhauls as part of owning the buses.

recognition: Ticket sales: contract liability (air traffic liability) until transportation is provided (ASC 606).
Loyalty points: separate performance obligation with deferred revenue.
Maintenance: expense-as-incurred, built-in overhaul, or deferral methods applied consistently.
Source library contains the Overall subtopic; industry subtopics are referenced.

measurement.initial: Allocate ticket price between transportation and loyalty points by standalone selling price.
measurement.subsequent: Recognize breakage on unused tickets under 606 breakage guidance.

journalEntries.label: Sell advance tickets
journalEntries.scenario: An airline sells $2,500,000 of tickets for flights next month.
journalEntries.memo: Revenue recognized when flown.

auditTraps.a: When the transportation is provided (flown), not when sold.

auditTraps.q: How is expected ticket breakage handled?
auditTraps.a: Recognized in proportion to the pattern of rights exercised if the airline expects to be entitled to breakage (606-10-55-48).
Slots with indefinite lives are not amortized but tested for impairment.

(g) Compensation—General (h) Other Expenses (i) Nonmonetary Transactions. Each Subtopic provides background on…

910.title: Contractors—Construction
910.tag: Construction contractors: contract costs, use rates for equipment, and retainage — revenue itself follows 606.
910.truth: A contractor's profit depends on accurately tracking the costs of each job. Revenue for construction contracts now follows ASC 606 (usually over time), but this Topic keeps industry guidance on which costs belong to contracts (equipment use rates, small tools, pre-contract costs) and on presenting retainage and contract balances.

analogy.title: The Custom Home Builder's Job Folders
analogy.story: A builder keeps one folder per house: lumber, labor, crane rental hours. Only by charging each cost to the right folder can she tell which houses make money — and the owner's 10% holdback (retainage) is money earned but not yet collectible.

recognition: Contract costs include direct costs and allocable indirect costs; construction equipment costs may be charged using use rates (910-20-25-1).
Revenue: ASC 606 — typically over time using a cost-to-cost input method when the customer controls the work in progress.
Retainage receivable/payable presented and disclosed; contract assets (underbillings) and contract liabilities (overbillings).
Anticipated losses on contracts are recognized immediately (605-35 remnant for provisions for losses).

measurement.basis: Cost-to-cost progress (606), contract costs at cost
measurement.initial: Measure progress as costs incurred ÷ total estimated costs.
measurement.subsequent: Update estimates each period with cumulative catch-up.

journalEntries.label: Owner's view: construction draw with 10% retainage
journalEntries.scenario: A developer approves a GC pay application for $500,000 with 10% retainage.
journalEntries.memo: Retainage is paid at substantial completion after lien waivers.

auditTraps.q: Is retainage a contingent liability for the owner?
auditTraps.a: No — it is a liability for work performed; only payment timing is deferred (release conditions).

auditTraps.q: Where does construction revenue guidance live now?
auditTraps.a: ASC 606; Topic 910 retains cost and presentation guidance.

auditTraps.q: When are losses on a fixed-price contract recognized?
auditTraps.a: As soon as the loss is evident — the full expected loss, not just the portion to date.

910.propertyLens: Development and renovation projects track GC draws, retainage and change orders in job-cost modules; contractors on the other side apply 910/606.

keyParagraphs.excerpt: Operating unit costs for construction equipment may be included in contract cost using the use rate theory.

912.title: Contractors—Federal Government
912.tag: Federal government contractors: cost-plus contracts, allowable costs and terminations.
912.truth: Selling to the federal government means dealing with a sovereign customer that sets cost rules (FAR/CAS), can audit, and can terminate for convenience. Contractors track allowable vs. unallowable costs carefully because revenue on cost-plus contracts depends on them, and termination claims are recognized when realization is probable.

analogy.title: The Reimbursed Business Trip
analogy.story: Your employer reimburses travel costs — but not the minibar. You carefully separate allowable from unallowable receipts because only the allowable ones come back, and an auditor may check.

recognition: Cost-plus revenue follows ASC 606, with variable fees estimated and constrained.
Unallowable costs are excluded from amounts billed to the government.
Termination-for-convenience claims recognized when realization is probable and estimable (912-20-25).

measurement.initial: Estimate award/incentive fees as variable consideration.
measurement.subsequent: Adjust for audit disallowances when probable.

journalEntries.label: Bill allowable costs plus fixed fee
journalEntries.scenario: A contractor incurs $900,000 of allowable costs; fixed fee earned is $54,000.
journalEntries.memo: Over-time recognition as costs are incurred.

auditTraps.a: No — they are expensed and excluded from government billings.
When realization is probable and the amount estimable — gain-contingency rules apply to amounts above cost.
Yes — contracts with the government are contracts with customers.

This unique behavior results from the customer being a sovereign power that conducts its procurement activities under specific laws and implementing regulations. These procurement statutes and regulations govern the process the federal government must…

915.title: Development Stage Entities
915.tag: Development stage entities — reporting requirements removed (ASU 2014-15); Topic is status-only.
915.truth: Start-ups once had to present inception-to-date information and label themselves 'development stage entities'. FASB removed the concept because it added cost without useful information — a young company follows the same GAAP as everyone else, with going-concern and risk disclosures doing the real work.

analogy.title: The Training Wheels Removed
analogy.story: Kids used to ride with training wheels labeled 'beginner'. Once the rules said everyone rides the same bike, the label disappeared — beginners just ride carefully and wear a helmet (going-concern and risk disclosures).

recognition: No separate recognition model: development-stage presentation requirements were removed by ASU 2014-15 (effective 2015).
Start-up costs are expensed under ASC 720-15; going-concern evaluation under ASC 205-40.
The source library holds only status content for this Topic.

measurement.initial: Apply the governing Topics.
measurement.subsequent: No inception-to-date presentation.

journalEntries.label: Organization costs of a new property-management venture
journalEntries.scenario: Legal and formation costs of $40,000 for a newly formed entity.
journalEntries.memo: Expensed under ASC 720-15; no development-stage labeling.

auditTraps.a: No — removed by ASU 2014-15.
Expensed as incurred (720-15).

auditTraps.q: Is a going-concern evaluation still required?
auditTraps.a: Yes, under ASC 205-40 for every entity.

920.title: Entertainment—Broadcasters
920.tag: Broadcasters: program rights and barter — Topic overview (industry subtopics referenced).
920.truth: A TV station buys rights to air programs and earns ad revenue when they air. Program rights are assets recognized when the license period begins and the program is available, amortized as aired; FCC licenses are intangibles often with indefinite lives.

analogy.title: The Movie-Night Subscription
analogy.story: A community theater buys the rights to show a film ten times this year. The rights are an asset when the film arrives and can be shown, and each screening uses part of the cost.

recognition: Recognize program rights as assets when the license period begins, the cost is known, the program is accepted and available for first showing (920-350).
Amortize based on estimated number of showings or revenue pattern.
FCC licenses: indefinite-lived intangibles tested for impairment.

measurement.initial: Initial: gross license fee (present value if significant financing).
measurement.subsequent: Subsequent: amortize; impairment to net realizable value.

journalEntries.label: Recognize available program rights
journalEntries.scenario: A station's license for a syndicated series ($600,000) becomes available for airing.
journalEntries.memo: Amortize as episodes air.

auditTraps.a: When the license period begins and all conditions are met — not at contract signing.
Typically not (indefinite life), but tested for impairment annually.
At fair value of goods/services received (606 noncash consideration).

keyParagraphs.excerpt: The Entertainment—Broadcasters Topic presents standards of financial accounting and reporting for broadcasters.

922.title: Entertainment—Cable Television
922.tag: Cable television: prematurity period and system construction costs — Topic overview.
922.truth: Building a cable system takes years before subscribers fill it. During the prematurity period, costs are allocated between the portion serving current subscribers (expensed) and the portion for future subscribers (capitalized), so early losses aren't overstated nor profits flattered.

analogy.title: Building a New Subdivision's Water Lines
analogy.story: A utility lays pipes for 1,000 homes when only 200 are occupied. Costs to serve those 200 are today's expense; the capacity for the future 800 is an investment.

recognition: During prematurity, capitalize system costs and allocate certain costs between current and future subscribers (922-360).
Initial hookup revenue recognized to the extent of direct selling costs; installation costs capitalized.
Franchise costs capitalized and amortized.

measurement.initial: Allocate prematurity costs by subscriber fraction.
measurement.subsequent: Depreciate plant over useful life.

journalEntries.label: Capitalize new-subscriber installation costs
journalEntries.scenario: Installation labor and materials for new drops cost $75,000.
journalEntries.memo: Depreciated over the estimated period of benefit.

auditTraps.a: The period before the system reaches break-even subscriber levels (usually ≤2 years) during which special cost allocation applies.
No — expensed as incurred.
Cable system operators; the source library contains only the Overall overview.

keyParagraphs.excerpt: The Entertainment—Cable Television Topic addresses the standards of financial accounting and reporting for costs and expenses applicable to the construction and operation of a cable television system.

924.title: Entertainment—Casinos
924.tag: Casinos: gaming chips, promotional allowances and base-jackpot accruals — Topic overview.
924.truth: Casinos hold customers' money as chips, promise progressive jackpots and give away free rooms and meals to gamblers. Outstanding chips are liabilities, progressive jackpots are accrued as the obligation builds (base jackpots only when won or unavoidable), and 'comps' are part of the gaming transaction under ASC 606.

analogy.title: Arcade Tokens
analogy.story: When you buy $20 of arcade tokens, the arcade owes you play (or a refund) until you spend them — the tokens in your pocket are the arcade's liability.

recognition: Chips in customers' hands are a liability.
Progressive jackpots accrued as the incremental amount builds; base jackpots not accrued if the casino can avoid payment by removing the machine.
Complimentaries: allocate gaming revenue to comps by standalone selling price (606).

measurement.initial: Gaming revenue is net of payouts.
measurement.subsequent: Update jackpot accruals as play occurs.

journalEntries.label: Accrue progressive jackpot increment
journalEntries.scenario: A progressive slot's jackpot meter increases by $30,000 during the month.
journalEntries.memo: Base jackpots are not accrued before being won when payment is avoidable.

auditTraps.a: No, if the casino can avoid paying by removing the game; incremental progressive amounts are accrued.
Gaming revenue is allocated to the comped goods/services (e.g., room revenue) under 606.
No — net win (wagers less payouts).

Guidance also is provided for the disclosure of geographic segments, if any. General background information about the…

926.title: Entertainment—Films
926.tag: Films: capitalize film costs, amortize using individual-film-forecast, test for impairment.
926.truth: A film costs a fortune before earning anything, and its revenue arrives unevenly over years through theaters, streaming and licensing. So production costs are capitalized and amortized in proportion to revenue as it's earned (individual-film-forecast method), with impairment testing when the film won't recover its cost.

analogy.title: The Self-Published Novel
analogy.story: An author spends $50,000 producing a book expected to earn $200,000 over five years. Each year, she expenses the share of production cost matching that year's share of total expected sales.

recognition: Report film costs as a separate asset (926-20-25-1); production overhead included; administrative/distribution costs excluded.
Amortize using the individual-film-forecast method (current revenue ÷ ultimate revenue) or monetized with a group of films.
Test for impairment when indicators exist (fair value, individually or in a film group).
Participation costs accrued as revenue is recognized.

measurement.basis: Capitalized cost less amortization and impairment
measurement.initial: Accumulate production costs, including capitalized interest where applicable.
measurement.subsequent: Amortize by revenue ratio; revise ultimate revenue estimates prospectively.

journalEntries.label: Amortize film costs
journalEntries.scenario: A $10,000,000 film expects $25,000,000 ultimate revenue; this year's revenue is $5,000,000 (20%).
journalEntries.memo: Individual-film-forecast method.

auditTraps.q: Are marketing costs capitalized into film costs?
auditTraps.a: No — exploitation/marketing costs are expensed as incurred (advertising).

auditTraps.q: How long can ultimate revenue be projected?
auditTraps.a: Generally up to 10 years from initial release (20 years for acquired libraries).
Individually, or at the film-group level when monetized as a group (e.g., streaming).

keyParagraphs.excerpt: An entity shall report film costs as a separate asset on its balance sheet.

928.title: Entertainment—Music
928.tag: Music: advances to artists and license fees for masters and copyrights — Topic overview.
928.truth: Record labels pay artists advances before knowing whether songs will sell. An advance is an asset only if past performance and current popularity make recovery from future royalties likely; otherwise it's expensed. Licensing revenue follows ASC 606's IP license guidance.

analogy.title: The Book Advance
analogy.story: A publisher advances a famous author $100,000 against future royalties — likely recoverable. The same advance to an unknown first-time author is closer to a bet, better expensed.

recognition: Capitalize artist advances when past performance and current popularity provide a sound basis for estimating recovery from future royalties.
Cost of record masters is capitalized when recoverable from future sales.
License revenue: ASC 606 IP licensing (functional IP at a point in time; sales-based royalties when sales occur).

measurement.initial: Advances recorded as assets to the extent recoverable.
measurement.subsequent: Charge to expense as royalties are earned; write down unrecoverable amounts.

journalEntries.label: Recoverable artist advance
journalEntries.scenario: A label pays a proven artist a $250,000 advance recoupable from royalties.
journalEntries.memo: Reduced as royalties are earned; expensed if recoupment becomes unlikely.

auditTraps.a: No — only if recovery is reasonably assured based on past performance and popularity.

auditTraps.q: How are sales-based royalties recognized by the licensor?
auditTraps.a: When the later of the sale or usage occurs and the performance obligation is satisfied (606 royalty exception).
The library contains the Overall subtopic only; industry subtopics are referenced in 928-10-05-1.

Such entities often enter into contractual agreements to license music copyrights or record masters. This Topic provides accounting guidance for such license agreements, as well as for artist compensation costs, for compensation paid to recording artists in the form of royalties, and for the costs of producing…

930.title: Extractive Activities—Mining
930.tag: Mining: exploration, development and production phases; stripping costs are production costs.
930.truth: Mining is a long bet on what lies underground. Exploration spending before proven reserves exist is usually expensed because the payoff is uncertain; costs to develop a proven mine are capitalized; and waste removal once production starts (stripping) is a cost of the ore extracted in that period.

analogy.title: Digging for a Buried Treasure Chest
analogy.story: Money spent searching the beach is a gamble (expensed). Once you've found the chest, the cost of digging the tunnel to reach it is part of the treasure's cost (capitalized). Shoveling sand while hauling it out is the cost of that day's haul.

recognition: Exploration costs generally expensed until reserves are established; mineral rights acquisition capitalized.
Development costs capitalized; depleted using units-of-production.
Stripping costs incurred during the production phase are variable production costs included in inventory (930-330).

measurement.initial: Capitalized development costs and mineral rights at cost.
measurement.subsequent: Deplete over proven and probable reserves.

journalEntries.label: Production-phase stripping costs
journalEntries.scenario: A producing mine incurs $400,000 of stripping costs this month.
journalEntries.memo: Production-phase stripping is inventoried, not capitalized as PP&E.

auditTraps.q: Are production-phase stripping costs capitalized to PP&E?
auditTraps.a: No — they are inventory production costs.
Generally expensed before reserves are established (differs from oil & gas successful-efforts rules).
Units-of-production based on reserves.

keyParagraphs.excerpt: This Subtopic provides overall guidance for extractive activities in the mining industry, including the identification of entities that fall within the scope of this Topic and definitions of industry terms.

932.title: Extractive Activities—Oil and Gas
932.tag: Oil and gas: successful efforts vs. full cost; reserves disclosures (SEC).
932.truth: Drilling is a lottery: some wells hit, many are dry. Successful-efforts accounting capitalizes only the costs tied to discoveries and expenses dry holes; the full-cost method (SEC-permitted) capitalizes all exploration costs in a country-wide pool subject to a ceiling test. Either way, reserve quantities drive depletion and must be disclosed.

analogy.title: Buying Lottery Tickets
analogy.story: Successful efforts: you only count the cost of winning tickets as your 'investment' and write off the losers. Full cost: you treat all tickets bought as the cost of your winnings, as long as winnings exceed the pile.

recognition: Successful efforts: capitalize acquisition and successful exploratory/development costs; expense geological & geophysical and dry-hole costs.
Full cost (SEC rules, Reg S-X 4-10): capitalize all costs in cost centers, subject to a quarterly ceiling test.
Supplementary reserve-quantity and standardized-measure disclosures (932-235).

measurement.initial: Capitalize per method.
measurement.subsequent: Deplete using proved (developed) reserves; impair under 360 (SE) or ceiling test (FC).

journalEntries.label: Expense a dry exploratory well (successful efforts)
journalEntries.scenario: An exploratory well costing $3,200,000 is found dry.
journalEntries.memo: Under full cost it would stay in the cost pool.

auditTraps.a: Successful efforts.

auditTraps.q: What is the full-cost ceiling test?
auditTraps.a: Capitalized costs less related deferred taxes cannot exceed the present value (10%) of future net revenues from proved reserves plus certain other amounts.
Supplementary reserve information is required but typically unaudited (SEC registrants).

940.title: Financial Services—Brokers and Dealers
940.tag: Broker-dealers: trade-date accounting, fair value of securities inventory and segregation of customer funds.
940.truth: Broker-dealers hold customers' cash and securities and trade for their own account. Their inventory is marked to fair value, customer assets are segregated by regulation, and commissions are earned when trades execute — all to show whether the firm can meet obligations to customers.

analogy.title: The Pawnbroker and the Currency Exchange
analogy.story: A currency booth holds customers' money briefly and also trades its own stash. Its own stash is valued at today's rates; customers' money must be kept separate and returned on demand.

recognition: Securities transactions recorded on trade date (940-320).
Proprietary securities inventory at fair value with changes in earnings.
Commission revenue recognized on trade date (606).
Customer cash and securities segregated per SEC Rule 15c3-3.

measurement.initial: Measure positions at fair value.
measurement.subsequent: Remeasure each period; unrealized gains/losses in earnings.

journalEntries.label: Mark proprietary inventory to fair value
journalEntries.scenario: A broker-dealer's trading inventory rises $120,000 in value.
journalEntries.memo: Unrealized gains through earnings.

auditTraps.a: Trade date for regular-way trades.

auditTraps.q: Are customer securities on the balance sheet?
auditTraps.a: Generally no — held in custody; customer cash payables and receivables are presented.
Research purchased with commissions must be accounted for and disclosed properly.

942.title: Financial Services—Depository and Lending
942.tag: Banks and lenders: industry presentation (SEC Article 9) — Topic overview with SEC materials.
942.truth: Banks turn deposits into loans. Their statements emphasize liquidity, credit quality and capital, so industry guidance governs how loans, deposits and regulatory capital are presented — while credit losses follow CECL (ASC 326) like everyone else.

analogy.title: The Community Lending Library
analogy.story: A library lends books it borrowed from members. Members can demand their books back anytime (deposits), while the library's loans come back slowly — so the library's report focuses on how many books are out, overdue, and how many it keeps on hand.

recognition: Loans at amortized cost with CECL allowance (326-20); loan fees under 310-20.
Deposits recognized as liabilities.
SEC registrants follow Regulation S-X Article 9 presentation (942-10-S99).

measurement.initial: Loans net of deferred fees and allowance.
measurement.subsequent: Update allowance each period.

journalEntries.label: Originate a commercial real estate loan
journalEntries.scenario: A bank funds a $5,000,000 multifamily loan and collects a $25,000 origination fee.
journalEntries.memo: Fee amortized into interest income (310-20).

auditTraps.q: Where are bank credit losses measured?
auditTraps.a: ASC 326 (CECL).

auditTraps.q: Are origination fees revenue at closing?
auditTraps.a: No — deferred and amortized as yield adjustments.
SEC Regulation S-X rules prescribing bank holding company statement formats and disclosures.

944.title: Financial Services—Insurance
944.tag: Insurance: premiums earned over coverage, claims reserves, deferred acquisition costs and LDTI.
944.truth: An insurer collects premiums today for promises that may come due years later. Premiums are earned over the coverage period, claims are reserved when insured events occur (including those incurred but not reported), and only successful acquisition costs are deferred. For long-duration contracts, LDTI requires updating assumptions so liabilities reflect current expectations.

analogy.title: The Neighborhood Umbrella Pool
analogy.story: Neighbors each pay $10 into a pool that buys an umbrella for anyone caught in rain this year. The pool 'earns' each $10 a little every day of the year, and when it rains, it must set aside money for umbrellas owed — even to neighbors who haven't reported getting wet yet (IBNR).

recognition: Short-duration premiums: recognized over the contract period in proportion to protection provided.
Claims liabilities (including IBNR) recognized when insured events occur.
Deferred acquisition costs: only incremental direct costs of successful contract acquisition (944-30).

Long-duration contracts (LDTI, ASU 2018-12): update cash-flow assumptions at least annually; discount rate from upper-medium-grade fixed-income yields (changes in OCI); market risk benefits at fair value.

measurement.basis: Unearned premium; claims at ultimate cost; LFPB with current assumptions
measurement.initial: Claims reserves at estimated ultimate cost (undiscounted for most short-duration).
measurement.subsequent: Premium deficiency tests; DAC amortized on a constant-level basis (LDTI).

journalEntries.label: Earn one month of an annual property policy (insurer's side)
journalEntries.scenario: An insurer wrote a $1,200,000 annual premium; one month is earned.
journalEntries.memo: Mirror image of the insured's prepaid insurance amortization.

auditTraps.a: Yes — incurred-but-not-reported claims are estimated and accrued.
Only incremental direct costs of successful contract acquisition (ASU 2010-26).

auditTraps.q: Under LDTI, where do discount-rate changes go?
auditTraps.a: OCI for the liability for future policy benefits (instrument-specific credit risk for MRBs also OCI).

946.title: Financial Services—Investment Companies
946.tag: Investment companies: everything at fair value, no consolidation of portfolio companies (real estate funds often qualify).
946.truth: An investment company exists to earn returns from capital appreciation and income — not to operate what it owns. So its investments, including controlling stakes and real estate, are measured at fair value, and it does not consolidate operating investees. 948.title: Financial Services—Mortgage Banking
948.tag: Mortgage banking: loans held for sale at lower of cost or fair value; servicing rights recognized.
948.truth: A mortgage banker originates loans to sell them, not to hold them. Loans held for sale are carried at the lower of cost or fair value (or fair value by election), and when loans are sold with servicing retained, the right to earn servicing fees is a separate asset.

950.truth: A title insurer's plant — the indexed history of ownership and liens on local parcels — doesn't wear out if maintained; it becomes more valuable as history accumulates. So construction or purchase costs are capitalized and not depreciated, while daily maintenance is expensed.

952.title: Franchisors

952.truth: A franchisor sells the right to use its brand and system. 958.truth: A nonprofit has no owners — donors fund a mission and may restrict how their gifts are used. 960.title: Plan Accounting—Defined Benefit Pension Plans
960.tag: Defined benefit pension plan accounting: net assets available for benefits and accumulated plan benefits.
960.truth: This Topic is the plan's own report (not the employer's): does the trust hold enough to pay promised benefits? It shows net assets available for benefits at fair value and the actuarial present value of accumulated plan benefits, so participants can judge the plan's ability to pay.

970.title: Real Estate—General
970.tag: Real estate—General: capitalize project costs (preacquisition, taxes, insurance, amenities), allocate them, and account for syndications.
970.truth: Building or redeveloping property is a long manufacturing process: land, permits, construction, taxes, insurance and interest all go into producing a finished asset that will earn rent or be sold. So those costs are capitalized into the project until it's substantially complete, then allocated to units or components — while costs of simply operating or marketing the property are expensed.

analogy.title: Baking a Wedding Cake
analogy.story: Everything that goes into the cake — flour, eggs, the baker's hours, even the oven's electricity while it bakes — is part of the cake's cost. Once the cake is on the table, keeping the room air-conditioned is a cost of the party, not the cake. Development costs are the ingredients; post-completion operating costs are the party.

recognition: Scope: all entities with productive activities relating to real property (970-10-15-3), except property used in non-real estate operations (970-10-15-8).
Preacquisition costs (options, surveys, zoning, traffic studies) are capitalized if directly identifiable with the property and acquisition is probable; otherwise expensed.
Property taxes and insurance are capitalized only while the property is undergoing development activities.
Project costs clearly associated with acquisition, development and construction are capitalized; indirect costs capitalized only if clearly related to projects under development.
Amenities: costs in excess of anticipated proceeds are allocated as common costs to the units benefited.
Incidental operations: net revenue reduces capitalized costs; net costs in excess of revenue are expensed (not capitalized).
Rental projects: capitalize costs until substantially complete and held available for occupancy (no later than one year from cessation of major construction), then expense carrying costs.
Source note: the library contains 970-10 (overview, scope and syndication/project-cost scope); the detailed rules live in 970-340, 970-360 and 970-835, which are referenced there (970-10-15-11).

auditTraps.q: Can property taxes on land held for future development with no activity be capitalized?
auditTraps.a: No — taxes and insurance are capitalized only while development activities are in progress; land simply held is carried without capitalizing carrying costs (they are expensed).

auditTraps.q: When does capitalization stop on a rental project?
auditTraps.a: When the project is substantially completed and held available for occupancy — no later than one year after major construction activity ends — even if lease-up is slow.

auditTraps.q: Are leasing and marketing costs for a new building capitalized?
auditTraps.a: Generally no — advertising and start-up costs are expensed (720); only costs directly related to construction are capitalized. Model units/furnishings follow their own analysis.

auditTraps.q: How is net income from a parking lot operated on the site before development (incidental operations) treated?
auditTraps.a: Net incidental revenue reduces capitalized project costs; net losses are expensed — never capitalized as 'negative income'.

auditTraps.q: Why can't my auditor find 970-340 in our library?
auditTraps.a: The source export includes only 970-10; 970-340/360/835 content is referenced by 970-10-15-11 and must be read in the full FASB Codification.

972.title: Real Estate—Common Interest Realty Associations
972.tag: Common interest realty associations (HOAs, condo associations): funds for future major repairs and common property.
972.truth: An HOA collects dues from owners to run and eventually rebuild shared property — roofs, pools, elevators. It rarely owns the common areas outright in a way it could sell, so they often aren't recognized as assets; instead, the statements show operating results and the funds set aside for future major repairs, with supplementary information on the reserve study.

974.title: Real Estate—Real Estate Investment Trusts
974.tag: REITs: distribute 90% of taxable income, disclose tax status of distributions, follow SEC Rule 3-15.
974.truth: A REIT is a tax-advantaged wrapper: it avoids corporate income tax if it distributes at least 90% of its taxable income and meets asset and income tests. The accounting is ordinary GAAP, but readers need to know the tax character of distributions (ordinary income, capital gain, return of capital) and how the REIT maintains its status.

recognition: A REIT that distributes ≥90% of taxable income (and meets other tests) is generally not subject to federal corporate income tax (974-10-05-4).

976.title: Real Estate—Retail Land
976.tag: Retail land sales: volume sales of subdivided lots with seller financing (revenue now under 606).
976.truth: Retail land companies sell lots from large subdivided tracts in high volume, often with small down payments and seller financing, and promise future improvements. Historically this called for installment and deposit methods; today revenue follows ASC 606, with collectibility and the obligation to complete improvements driving timing.

analogy.title: Selling Plots in a Lakeside Development
analogy.story: A developer sells 500 lakeside lots with 10% down, promising to pave roads next year. It's not done selling until the promised roads are built, and it can't count on collecting from buyers who might walk away from small deposits.

recognition: Scope: retail land sales on a volume basis of lots from subdivided tracts (976-10-05-2).
Revenue under ASC 606: contract existence (including collectibility of substantially all consideration) and performance obligations for promised improvements.
Legacy 976-605 installment/deposit methods were superseded by ASU 2014-09.

measurement.initial: Allocate consideration to lot and improvement obligations.
measurement.subsequent: Recognize improvement obligations as performed.

journalEntries.label: Sale of a lot with an obligation to build roads
journalEntries.scenario: A $60,000 lot sale ($6,000 cash, $54,000 note); $8,000 of the price is allocated to the road-completion obligation.
journalEntries.memo: Collectibility must be probable for a contract to exist under 606.

auditTraps.q: Is the installment method still used for GAAP?
auditTraps.a: No — superseded by ASC 606; collectibility is assessed at contract inception.
As performance obligations (or costs to fulfill) — revenue allocated to them is deferred until performed.
The library holds only 976-10 overview/scope content.

976.propertyLens: Multifamily developers rarely sell retail lots, but master-planned communities that sell land parcels to homebuilders use the same 606 collectibility and improvement-obligation logic.

keyParagraphs.excerpt: The Real Estate—Retail Land Topic addresses the unique accounting and reporting issues for retail land sales that are sales, on a volume basis, of lots that are subdivisions of large tracts of land. The sales are characterized by very small down payments and a sales contract or buyer's note for the balance of the purchase price. This Topic includes the following Subtopics: (a) Overall (b) Receivables (c) Inventory…

978.title: Real Estate—Time-Sharing Activities
978.tag: Time-sharing: account for each phase separately; uncollectibility reduces revenue; heavy selling costs.
978.truth: Timeshare sellers market intervals in volume, finance most buyers and expect meaningful defaults — when buyers default, the seller recovers and resells the interval. So projects are tracked by phase, expected uncollectibility is treated as a reduction of revenue, and inventory costs are relieved using a relative sales-value method.

analogy.title: Selling Weeks at a Beach Condo
analogy.story: A developer sells 52 separate weeks of one condo to 52 families, financing most of them. Some families will stop paying and give their week back — the developer plans for that from the start and resells those weeks.

recognition: Establish and delineate a project and its phases at the outset; account for each phase separately (978-10-25-1).
Revenue under 606 (legacy 978 profit-recognition methods superseded); estimated uncollectibility of notes receivable reduces revenue (variable consideration).
Cost of sales and inventory using the relative sales value method, with recoveries of defaulted intervals considered.

measurement.initial: Transaction price net of expected uncollectibility.
measurement.subsequent: True up via cumulative adjustments to cost of sales as estimates change.

journalEntries.label: Sell a timeshare interval with seller financing
journalEntries.scenario: Interval sold for $30,000: $3,000 down, $27,000 note; expected uncollectibility $2,700 reduces revenue.
journalEntries.memo: Expected defaults reduce revenue, not bad-debt expense.

auditTraps.a: No — estimated uncollectibility is a reduction of revenue under the Topic's model.
Relative sales value method, reflecting expected recoveries of repossessed intervals.

auditTraps.q: Are selling and marketing costs capitalized?
auditTraps.a: Generally expensed as incurred; limited costs related to unsold intervals may be deferred when directly tied to future sales.

978.propertyLens: Operators that convert apartment buildings to vacation-ownership or short-term rental programs meet time-sharing concepts; the phase-by-phase and seller-financing logic mirrors condo-conversion sell-outs.

keyParagraphs.excerpt: As indicated in paragraph 978-10-15-6, a time-share seller shall establish and delineate a project and its phases at the outset of the project and each phase shall be accounted for separately.

980.title: Regulated Operations
980.tag: Regulated operations: rate regulation can turn costs into regulatory assets (and refunds into regulatory liabilities).
980.truth: When a regulator sets a utility's prices based on its costs and promises it will recover a cost through future rates, that cost is effectively a receivable from future customers — a regulatory asset — rather than an expense today. The reverse (amounts to be refunded) is a regulatory liability.

analogy.title: The Parent-Approved Allowance Advance
analogy.story: A teen buys a school laptop with her own savings after her parents promise to raise her allowance next year to cover it. The laptop cost isn't truly 'spent' — it will come back through future allowance.

recognition: Apply when rates are set by a regulator, designed to recover the entity's specific costs, and it is reasonable to assume rates can be charged and collected (980-10-15-2).
Capitalize incurred costs as regulatory assets when it is probable future revenue will recover them.
Recognize regulatory liabilities for amounts to be refunded or future costs collected in advance.
Discontinue 980 accounting (980-20) when criteria are no longer met; write off regulatory assets/liabilities.

measurement.initial: Regulatory assets at incurred cost expected to be recovered.
measurement.subsequent: Amortize as recovered in rates; test for probability of recovery each period.

journalEntries.label: Defer storm-restoration costs approved for recovery
journalEntries.scenario: A utility incurs $8,000,000 of storm costs the commission has approved for recovery in future rates.
journalEntries.memo: Amortized to expense as recovered through rates.

auditTraps.a: No — criteria require cost-based rate regulation with probable recovery.
Discontinue 980 (980-20): eliminate regulatory assets/liabilities through earnings.
Yes — they must remain probable of recovery; otherwise written off.

985.title: Software
985.tag: Software for sale: expense until technological feasibility, then capitalize and amortize.
985.truth: Building software to sell is R&D until the company knows it can be built — technological feasibility. After that, coding and testing costs create a product asset that is capitalized and amortized as the software is sold, with a net realizable value check.

analogy.title: Writing a Video Game
analogy.story: Brainstorming and prototyping game ideas is research — much of it will be scrapped. Once you have a detailed design proven to work, the hours spent building the final game create something you'll sell for years.

recognition: Costs before technological feasibility (detailed program design or working model) are R&D expense (985-20-25-1).
Capitalize production costs after feasibility until the product is available for general release.
Amortize the greater of the revenue ratio or straight-line over remaining life; compare to NRV each period.

measurement.basis: Capitalized cost less amortization, limited to NRV
measurement.initial: Capitalize direct costs after feasibility.
measurement.subsequent: Amortization method: greater of ratio of current revenue or straight-line.

journalEntries.label: Capitalize post-feasibility development costs
journalEntries.scenario: A software company incurs $900,000 of coding and testing after establishing technological feasibility.
journalEntries.memo: Amortized from general release.

auditTraps.a: No — internal-use software follows 350-40; 985-20 is for software to be sold, leased or marketed.
When a detailed program design is complete (or a working model exists) — in agile practice this is often very late, so little is capitalized.
SaaS offered as a service (customer can't take possession) is generally internal-use software (350-40).

995.title: U.S. Steamship Entities
995.tag: U.S. steamship entities: legacy deferred-tax guidance on statutory reserve deposits — now superseded (995-740).
995.truth: US shipping companies could deposit earnings in government-sanctioned construction funds to defer taxes. Special accounting once addressed the deferred taxes on these deposits; ASU 2017-15 removed the exception so the general ASC 740 model applies.

analogy.title: The Tax-Advantaged College Savings Plan
analogy.story: Money saved in a special plan defers tax until withdrawn — but the family still owes tax eventually. GAAP now simply records that future tax like any other deferred tax.

recognition: Topic content (995-740) was superseded by ASU 2017-15; entities apply ASC 740 deferred-tax guidance.
The source library holds status content only.

measurement.initial: Recognize deferred taxes on differences created by fund deposits.
measurement.subsequent: Remeasure for rate changes.

journalEntries.label: Deferred tax on capital construction fund deposits
journalEntries.scenario: A steamship entity's fund deposits create a $2,000,000 taxable temporary difference at a 21% rate.
journalEntries.memo: General ASC 740 model — no industry exception.

auditTraps.q: Is there still a steamship tax exception?
auditTraps.a: No — ASU 2017-15 eliminated it.
General accounting under ASC 740 (Income Taxes) now applies; the industry-specific exception was completely eliminated.
